relations.mechanism: An exception that reaches the process boundary can terminate a Windows application and produce a WER fault record.
when: The failure time aligns with a WER application-error record.
symptoms: Application exits unexpectedly.
counter: A clean application exit without a matching fault record weakens this mechanism.
limits: WER absence does not exclude a crash when reporting is disabled or unavailable.

relations.mechanism: A repeatedly identified faulting module can localize the failing code path within an application process.
when: Multiple WER records identify the same module and compatible application version.
symptoms: Repeated crashes at similar execution points.
counter: Different faulting modules across incidents argue against a single module explanation.
limits: The named module can be where failure surfaced rather than the original defect.

relations.mechanism: CPU, memory, or handle pressure can delay message processing until an application appears unresponsive.
when: Resource pressure overlaps the observed hang interval.
symptoms: Not responding state or long UI latency.
counter: Normal process and system resource levels throughout the hang weaken pressure as the cause.
limits: A hang can also result from deadlock or blocked external I/O.

relations.mechanism: A required file that is unavailable, locked, or denied can make application startup or save operations fail.
when: The application reports file access failure for a required resource.
symptoms: Startup failure, save failure, or partial feature failure.
counter: Successful access to the same file under the same identity weakens this explanation.
limits: The snapshot does not authorize opening arbitrary paths or changing permissions.

relations.mechanism: Applications that use a failing device stack can surface driver or device failures as application errors.
when: The application depends on the affected device and timestamps align.
symptoms: Crash, timeout, or feature unavailable.
counter: The application fails identically with the device path unused.
limits: Temporal alignment and dependency are required; co-occurrence alone is not causal evidence.

relations.mechanism: A missing or incompatible runtime dependency can prevent application initialization before normal logging begins.
when: The failure occurs during load and runtime inventory shows a relevant mismatch.
symptoms: Immediate startup exit or loader error.
counter: A successful load of the same binary and dependencies weakens this mechanism.
limits: Exact binary dependency resolution requires evidence not supplied by a generic snapshot.

relations.mechanism: The Service Control Manager can withhold or fail a dependent service when its declared prerequisite is unavailable.
when: A real configured dependency is stopped or failed before the dependent service.
symptoms: Dependent service start failure.
counter: All declared dependencies are running and healthy before the attempt.
limits: Undeclared application-level dependencies will not appear in SCM relationships.

relations.mechanism: A service that does not report progress within the control manager interval can be recorded as a start or control timeout.
when: SCM timeout events align with the control request.
symptoms: Service remains start-pending or request fails.
counter: The service promptly reaches running state on the same attempt.
limits: The timeout does not identify why the service failed to make progress.

relations.mechanism: A service account that cannot log on prevents creation of the service process under that identity.
when: SCM reports a logon failure for the configured service identity.
symptoms: Service fails before its normal application initialization.
counter: The service process is running under the intended account.
limits: The pack does not expose credentials or authorize identity changes.

relations.mechanism: A service that depends on a driver-backed device can fail when that driver service is unavailable.
when: A declared or documented device dependency exists and the driver failed first.
symptoms: Service starts partially or reports hardware unavailable.
counter: The service works with the same driver state or does not use that device.
limits: A device-category match alone is not evidence of dependency.

relations.mechanism: Services that must create logs, databases, or temporary state can fail when their target volume lacks space.
when: Low free capacity overlaps writes required by the service.
symptoms: Startup failure or write errors.
counter: Adequate free space and successful required writes weaken capacity as the cause.
limits: Generic free-space data does not identify each service write target.

relations.mechanism: Security or management policy can place a component in a disabled or passive state that appears as a service failure.
when: Effective policy and service state change together.
symptoms: Service disabled, stopped, or unable to enable a feature.
counter: No relevant policy is effective and the service configuration is unchanged.
limits: Policy precedence can require product-specific evidence beyond the snapshot.

relations.mechanism: Runnable work concentrated in one or more processes can sustain high processor utilization.
when: Per-process CPU use accounts for system CPU pressure during the incident.
symptoms: Slow response and high CPU utilization.
counter: System CPU is normal or the named processes do not account for measured load.
limits: A snapshot can miss short spikes and does not explain why work is expensive.

relations.mechanism: Growing process commit can consume the commit limit and increase paging or allocation failures.
when: Process memory growth precedes system commit pressure.
symptoms: Low-memory signals, paging, or allocation failure.
counter: Commit remains well below its limit throughout the incident.
limits: Working set alone is not equivalent to private commit or a memory leak.

relations.mechanism: Unbounded handle creation can exhaust per-process or system object resources and degrade operations.
when: Handle count grows over repeated observations without corresponding workload growth.
symptoms: Resource errors or gradual degradation.
counter: Handle counts remain stable across comparable workload intervals.
limits: A high stable count is not itself proof of a leak.

relations.mechanism: Heavy paging and allocation contention can delay application threads enough to appear hung.
when: Commit pressure and paging overlap the unresponsive interval.
symptoms: Long pauses or not-responding state.
counter: No memory pressure is observed before or during the hang.
limits: A deadlock can produce the same symptom without resource pressure.

relations.mechanism: Sustained processor activity prevents deep idle residency and increases energy use.
when: High CPU activity persists during the battery-drain interval.
symptoms: Reduced battery life or increased heat.
counter: The processor remains mostly idle during the affected interval.
limits: Battery health and device power can dominate total drain.

relations.mechanism: Termination of a service-hosting process makes one or more hosted services transition out of running state.
when: The service maps to the process identity and its exit time aligns.
symptoms: One or multiple services stop unexpectedly.
counter: The service is hosted by a different live process identity.
limits: PID reuse requires creation time or equivalent identity evidence.

relations.mechanism: An explicit PnP problem code records that Windows could not configure, start, or retain a device normally.
when: The affected device instance has a nonzero problem code.
symptoms: Device or dependent feature unavailable.
counter: The exact device instance reports present, started, and no problem code.
limits: The problem code narrows state but may not identify the underlying hardware or driver defect.

relations.mechanism: A PnP reconfiguration marked as requiring restart can leave the device unavailable until the transition completes.
when: The exact device reports CM_PROB_NEED_RESTART after configuration change.
symptoms: Feature remains unavailable after driver or device change.
counter: The device is started successfully after the same configuration change.
limits: Restart-required state does not prove all observed failures share that cause.

relations.mechanism: A device resource conflict can prevent Windows from assigning sufficient resources to start the device.
when: The exact device reports CM_PROB_NORMAL_CONFLICT or insufficient resources.
symptoms: Device start failure.
counter: The device starts with assigned resources and no conflict code.
limits: Modern systems can surface generic resource codes for multiple low-level causes.

relations.mechanism: A driver entry, AddDevice, or start failure can make PnP record a problem on the matching device instance.
when: Driver and device identifiers match and SetupAPI or problem-code timing aligns.
symptoms: Problem code 10, 31, 37, or related driver state.
counter: The matching driver loads and the device starts normally.
limits: Name similarity without a real device identifier is insufficient matching evidence.

relations.mechanism: A service with a real dependency on an unavailable device can fail initialization or lose a feature.
when: The service owns or explicitly uses the exact unavailable device.
symptoms: Hardware-backed service reports unavailable.
counter: No service-device dependency exists or the service works without the device.
limits: Category co-occurrence must not be treated as a dependency edge.

relations.mechanism: A device that fails a power-state transition can be temporarily unavailable after sleep or resume.
when: Unavailability begins at resume and matching device power events are present.
symptoms: Device missing or nonfunctional only after resume.
counter: The device remains unavailable across cold boot or has a persistent install problem.
limits: Power transition evidence is needed to distinguish resume-specific from persistent failure.

relations.mechanism: An installation failure can leave no associated service or an incomplete driver package for a device.
when: SetupAPI records an error for the exact package and device instance.
symptoms: Driver does not load or device has no selected driver.
counter: SetupAPI records successful installation of the active matching package.
limits: Historical install errors may be stale relative to the current active driver.

relations.mechanism: A package that does not support the device, OS build, or architecture can fail selection or startup.
when: Hardware IDs and package applicability do not match the active platform.
symptoms: No suitable driver or driver start failure.
counter: The active package explicitly supports the device and current OS architecture.
limits: Version difference alone is not proof of incompatibility.

relations.mechanism: Driver-handled hardware errors can surface through WHEA or device events while software is interacting with hardware.
when: The WHEA source and device topology match the driver-controlled hardware.
symptoms: Corrected or fatal hardware error event.
counter: Hardware errors persist with a different known-good driver path or before driver initialization.
limits: WHEA evidence can indicate hardware, firmware, bus, or driver interaction and is not automatically a driver defect.

relations.mechanism: A driver that delays or fails device power callbacks can lengthen or prevent system resume.
when: Power traces attribute delay to the matching device stack.
symptoms: Resume delay or device unavailable after wake.
counter: Trace timing shows the device stack completes promptly.
limits: A generic post-resume driver event without timing attribution is weak evidence.

relations.mechanism: A staged driver replacement can leave the previous driver active until restart, producing version or behavior mismatch.
when: Driver servicing reports restart required and active versus staged versions differ.
symptoms: Issue persists until the staged transition completes.
counter: No pending driver action exists and active package matches the installed package.
limits: A pending restart can be unrelated to the affected driver.

relations.mechanism: An application waiting synchronously on a stalled device request can appear hung while the driver stack makes no progress.
when: The application uses the device and wait timing aligns with driver errors.
symptoms: Application not responding during device I/O.
counter: The hang reproduces without device I/O or the driver stack completes normally.
limits: Confirming a blocked I/O stack usually requires deeper trace evidence.

relations.mechanism: A volume without sufficient free clusters cannot satisfy file growth or new allocation requests.
when: The target volume is near capacity when the write fails.
symptoms: Write, update, or temporary-file failure.
counter: The exact target volume has ample space and the allocation succeeds.
limits: System-wide free space does not identify the target volume for every operation.

relations.mechanism: An offline or missing disk makes its volumes and files unavailable to applications.
when: The target file resides on the exact offline or missing volume.
symptoms: Path not found or volume unavailable.
counter: The target volume is online, mounted, and accessible.
limits: A path can fail for permission or namespace reasons even when storage is online.

relations.mechanism: Retries and remapping around failing media can increase I/O completion latency.
when: Media or controller errors align with latency on the same physical disk.
symptoms: Slow reads or writes and storage warnings.
counter: No errors exist and latency is attributable to queueing from known workload.
limits: Generic disk latency cannot distinguish media from workload or controller causes.

relations.mechanism: Synchronous application I/O waits can stall UI or worker threads while storage latency is elevated.
when: The application accesses the affected volume during the hang interval.
symptoms: Long pauses correlated with disk latency.
counter: The application performs no I/O to the affected storage during the hang.
limits: Correlation requires matching time and target; system disk activity alone is insufficient.

relations.mechanism: Recovery, integrity checking, or repeated failed metadata operations can add file-system I/O latency.
when: File-system events and latency refer to the same volume and interval.
symptoms: Slow access and file-system warnings.
counter: The volume is healthy and latency is explained by workload queue depth.
limits: File-system events can be consequences of lower storage faults rather than the origin.

relations.mechanism: Windows servicing requires workspace for download, staging, and component updates; insufficient target capacity can stop the operation.
when: Servicing failure overlaps low capacity on the relevant system or reserved volume.
symptoms: Download, staging, or installation failure.
counter: Relevant volumes have sufficient capacity throughout servicing.
limits: Free-space thresholds vary by update and configuration.

relations.mechanism: Metadata inconsistency or detected corruption can prevent normal open, enumerate, read, write, or delete operations.
when: The file and error belong to the exact affected volume.
symptoms: File operation fails despite valid namespace and identity.
counter: The same operation succeeds and the volume reports no consistency errors.
limits: Access control and sharing violations can produce similar failures without corruption.

relations.mechanism: Unreadable or incorrectly persisted sectors can damage or make file-system metadata unavailable.
when: Media errors map to the physical storage backing the affected volume.
symptoms: NTFS or ReFS integrity events.
counter: Storage diagnostics are healthy and errors are reproducibly software-only.
limits: File-system corruption can also follow crashes or software defects.

relations.mechanism: ReFS checksum and repair signals distinguish integrity handling from generic path or permission errors.
when: The affected volume is ReFS and relevant ReFS events are present.
symptoms: Integrity warning, repair, or inaccessible data.
counter: The volume is not ReFS or no integrity signal refers to it.
limits: ReFS integrity signals do not by themselves identify the faulty hardware layer.

relations.mechanism: ACL denial or a conflicting open handle can reject an operation while the file system remains consistent.
when: The exact operation reports access denied or sharing violation.
symptoms: Cannot open, modify, rename, or delete a file.
counter: The same identity obtains required access and no conflicting handle exists.
limits: The reference pack does not enumerate arbitrary paths or expose ACL contents.

relations.mechanism: Loss of the backing disk can make a volume appear unavailable without an intrinsic on-disk file-system defect.
when: Disk offline state precedes loss of the volume.
symptoms: Volume missing or inaccessible.
counter: The disk and volume remain online while consistency errors are recorded.
limits: An offline state can itself follow a lower-level hardware failure.

relations.mechanism: Servicing can defer replacement of in-use system files until restart, leaving the pre-restart version active.
when: The affected component has a pending file operation and servicing requires restart.
symptoms: Old version remains loaded or update cannot finalize.
counter: No pending action exists and the expected file version is active.
limits: A pending restart elsewhere does not establish a relation to the affected file.

relations.mechanism: A rejected wireless authentication can prevent authenticated network access even if radio association succeeds.
when: A recent failure reason refers to the same WLAN interface and incident interval as the failed connection.
symptoms: The expected wireless connection is unavailable for network traffic.
counter: The interface has authenticated access during the affected interval.
limits: Association and enterprise authentication are distinct stages; the bounded event window may omit the cause, and an access point or authentication server can need external corroboration.

relations.mechanism: A client that has not associated with its intended Wi-Fi network cannot use that radio path to reach a destination.
when: The affected workload depends on that WLAN interface and no working alternate path is in use.
symptoms: The user reports no connection through the intended Wi-Fi network.
counter: The interface is associated and another stage, such as IP, DNS, proxy, or service access, fails instead.
limits: Association state is local configuration evidence, not an end-to-end reachability measurement.

relations.mechanism: A connected interface without an address or route usable for the target may fail before DNS or application traffic reaches the destination.
when: The expected interface is associated but lacks an appropriate IP address or destination route during the symptom.
symptoms: Local association succeeds but destination access fails.
counter: The interface has a usable address and a route selected for the destination.
limits: A missing default gateway may be normal for a restricted or local-only network; active reachability and target-specific routing need separate checks.

relations.mechanism: A missing or less-specific route can send traffic to an unreachable or unintended gateway.
when: The active route selected for the destination conflicts with the intended interface or gateway.
symptoms: Destination timeout or unreachable result.
counter: The selected route and gateway are correct and reachable.
limits: The passive connectivity snapshot lists default IPv4 routes only; the full bounded route table and a target-specific route selection are needed before attributing this mechanism. A correct route does not prove the remote service or firewall path is healthy.

relations.mechanism: A Windows Filtering Platform rule or default filter can explicitly discard traffic before the application receives it.
when: A matching WFP drop identifies the same application, interface, and flow.
symptoms: Connection timeout or refused access.
counter: No matching drop occurs and packets traverse the host firewall.
limits: Filter IDs can change; origin and flow context are needed for attribution.

relations.mechanism: Only one incompatible listener can bind a local address and port combination, preventing the intended service from listening.
when: Another live process owns the exact required endpoint.
symptoms: Bind error, absent listener, or connection refused.
counter: The intended process owns the endpoint or binding permits sharing.
limits: A listener on the same numeric port but different address or protocol may not conflict.

relations.mechanism: An application can report a general network timeout when it cannot resolve the destination name before connecting.
when: Name resolution fails before any destination connection attempt.
symptoms: Host not found or connection timeout.
counter: The destination resolves correctly and connection fails by IP address in the same way.
limits: Application messages may collapse DNS and connection phases into one error.

relations.mechanism: Applications using WinHTTP or another proxy scope can fail while direct network connectivity remains healthy.
when: The failing application uses the affected proxy configuration.
symptoms: Selective HTTP or HTTPS failure.
counter: The application is configured for direct access or succeeds through the same proxy.
limits: Different Windows networking stacks can use different proxy settings.

relations.mechanism: Transport connection can succeed while TLS authentication fails before application data is exchanged.
when: A TCP connection is established and Schannel reports handshake or validation failure.
symptoms: HTTPS or secure-protocol connection fails.
counter: No transport connection is established or TLS completes successfully.
limits: Generic connectivity snapshots may not capture the complete handshake transcript.

relations.mechanism: A Windows DNS query can time out when routing or gateway state prevents reaching the configured DNS server.
when: The configured resolver address is unreachable through the selected route.
symptoms: DNS timeout for multiple names.
counter: The resolver is reachable and answers direct queries promptly.
limits: ICMP reachability alone does not prove DNS service availability.

relations.mechanism: A cached negative answer can make repeated Windows DNS lookups fail until the negative cache entry expires or changes.
when: The failing name has a cached negative response matching the resolver result.
symptoms: Name continues to fail after the authoritative record changes.
counter: No negative entry exists or a direct authoritative query also fails identically.
limits: The snapshot must preserve cache timing to distinguish stale from current answers.

relations.mechanism: A short Windows host name can fail when the connection-specific suffix search does not construct the intended FQDN.
when: FQDN resolution succeeds while the short name fails under the active suffix list.
symptoms: Internal short name not found.
counter: Both the short name and FQDN fail or suffix configuration is correct.
limits: Search behavior can vary with application and name-resolution API.

relations.mechanism: Automatic proxy discovery and named proxies can fail when required WPAD or proxy host names do not resolve.
when: The proxy path depends on the failing DNS name.
symptoms: Proxy discovery delay or proxy connection failure.
counter: The proxy is addressed directly or all required names resolve.
limits: Proxy discovery has additional policy and DHCP inputs not represented by DNS alone.

relations.mechanism: The destination host name produced by resolution is also the identity normally checked against a TLS server certificate.
when: TLS server authentication uses the requested DNS host name.
symptoms: Resolution succeeds but certificate name validation fails.
counter: The certificate contains the requested identity or the protocol uses a different verified identity.
limits: DNS success does not establish certificate trust or endpoint ownership.

relations.mechanism: A synchronous name-resolution call can block an application thread while resolver retries reach their timeout.
when: The hang duration and call path align with repeated DNS timeouts.
symptoms: UI or request stalls before connecting.
counter: Resolution is asynchronous or completes promptly during the hang.
limits: Thread-level trace evidence is needed for strong attribution.

relations.mechanism: WinHTTP automatic proxy discovery can delay or fail when PAC or WPAD discovery inputs are unavailable.
when: The application uses AutoProxy and discovery cannot obtain or evaluate its configuration.
symptoms: Initial HTTP request delay or proxy discovery error.
counter: A valid cached PAC result is used or the application is configured directly.
limits: Application frameworks may not use WinHTTP proxy discovery.

relations.mechanism: A stale proxy address or bypass rule can send requests to an unavailable intermediary or unintended path.
when: The failing application uses the exact affected proxy scope.
symptoms: HTTP requests fail selectively by destination.
counter: Effective configuration points to a reachable proxy and correct bypass decision.
limits: User, WinHTTP, and application proxy scopes can differ.

relations.mechanism: A proxy that intercepts or terminates TLS can change the certificate chain observed by the client.
when: The failing route traverses an intercepting proxy and the presented issuer changes.
symptoms: Certificate trust or identity error only through proxy.
counter: The same certificate chain is presented on direct and proxy paths.
limits: The generic snapshot may not expose full certificate chains.

relations.mechanism: Management policy can override local proxy preferences, yielding an effective configuration different from user expectation.
when: Effective managed settings differ from the local configuration.
symptoms: Proxy reverts or differs across applications.
counter: No relevant managed policy is applied and effective settings match.
limits: Policy provenance may require management-specific inventory beyond current probes.

relations.mechanism: DNS failure for WPAD or PAC host names can prevent automatic discovery from completing.
when: Discovery uses a name whose resolution fails in the same interval.
symptoms: AutoProxy timeout or direct fallback.
counter: Discovery obtains configuration without DNS or the required names resolve.
limits: DHCP-based discovery and cached scripts can bypass this mechanism.

relations.mechanism: Windows update retrieval can fail when its network stack cannot reach required endpoints through the effective proxy path.
when: Servicing download errors align with proxy failure and direct local servicing remains healthy.
symptoms: Update download or scan connectivity failure.
counter: Update endpoints are reachable through the same effective proxy.
limits: Update failure can occur after download for unrelated servicing reasons.

relations.mechanism: Schannel server authentication fails when the certificate chain cannot terminate at a trusted root under the active policy.
when: Chain validation identifies an untrusted root or incomplete chain.
symptoms: Secure connection rejected before application data.
counter: The presented chain builds to an accepted trust anchor.
limits: Trust stores and policy can differ by identity and process context.

relations.mechanism: Certificate validation rejects a chain when current time falls outside a certificate validity interval.
when: System time and certificate validity interval conflict.
symptoms: Expired or not-yet-valid certificate error.
counter: System time is correct and every certificate is within validity.
limits: A correct local clock does not exclude remote chain or revocation problems.

relations.mechanism: Server authentication fails when the requested host identity does not match identities asserted by the leaf certificate.
when: The requested DNS name is absent from accepted certificate identities.
symptoms: Certificate name mismatch.
counter: The requested identity matches a valid certificate identity.
limits: Applications can implement additional or different identity validation.

relations.mechanism: Failure to resolve the secure endpoint prevents reaching TLS, even when the application reports a generic secure connection error.
when: No endpoint connection occurs because name resolution fails first.
symptoms: HTTPS connection failure without handshake evidence.
counter: TCP connection and TLS negotiation begin with the resolved endpoint.
limits: Application error text may not distinguish connection phases.

relations.mechanism: Incorrect time or invalid endpoint certificate dates can prevent authenticated update transport.
when: Update connectivity fails with certificate-time validation evidence.
symptoms: Secure update download failure.
counter: TLS validation succeeds to the update endpoint.
limits: Servicing failures after transport are unrelated to this mechanism.

relations.mechanism: A filtered TLS flow can end before handshake completion and appear to the application as a secure-channel timeout.
when: A matching WFP drop occurs on the handshake flow.
symptoms: Handshake timeout without certificate validation result.
counter: Handshake packets traverse the host and Schannel records a validation error instead.
limits: Host firewall evidence does not cover upstream network filtering.

relations.mechanism: Modern Standby resume proceeds through device and PDC phases; a slow device transition can dominate exit latency.
when: Power trace attributes resume duration to the matching device phase.
symptoms: Screen-on or network readiness delayed after wake.
counter: The device phase completes promptly and delay occurs elsewhere.
limits: A normal post-resume device event without duration is not enough.

relations.mechanism: Recurring software activity can wake the platform or prevent sustained low-power residency during Modern Standby.
when: Activity overlaps low-power exits in the standby interval.
symptoms: Reduced low-power residency and battery drain.
counter: The system remains in its lowest power state for the expected interval.
limits: Current cheap probes do not replace a SleepStudy or ETW power trace.

relations.mechanism: Re-enabling network connectivity is a documented common source of Modern Standby resume latency.
when: Resume delay is localized to network restoration phases.
symptoms: System wakes but network remains unavailable or delays readiness.
counter: Network device and connectivity restore promptly.
limits: Network failure outside resume does not establish a power-transition cause.

relations.mechanism: Device power transitions depend on the device stack completing requested state changes.
when: The exact driver stack records failure during the sleep or resume transition.
symptoms: Delayed transition or device unavailable after wake.
counter: The stack completes the transition without error.
limits: Firmware and hardware can fail below a healthy driver.

relations.mechanism: Thermal or power limiting can reduce available processor performance so ordinary work consumes a larger share of capacity.
when: Hardware telemetry shows limiting while clocks or throughput fall.
symptoms: High utilization with reduced performance.
counter: No thermal or power limit is active and frequency remains expected.
limits: CPU utilization alone cannot identify throttling.

relations.mechanism: High active power can increase heat and trigger platform power or thermal control, coupling battery and performance symptoms.
when: Power draw, temperature, and limiting overlap under the same workload.
symptoms: Short battery life, heat, and reduced performance.
counter: Thermal state remains normal and drain occurs during low activity.
limits: Battery wear can reduce runtime without high platform power.

relations.mechanism: WHEA can record corrected or uncorrected memory errors reported by platform hardware.
when: The hardware error source identifies memory or memory-controller context.
symptoms: Corrected error event, crash, or instability.
counter: No matching WHEA memory record exists across affected intervals.
limits: WHEA source interpretation can require firmware and vendor detail.

relations.mechanism: PCI Express error reporting can surface bus or endpoint faults through WHEA records.
when: The record identifies the affected PCIe hierarchy or endpoint.
symptoms: Corrected bus error, device reset, or fatal hardware event.
counter: The record identifies a different hardware source.
limits: A PCIe error can originate in endpoint, link, firmware, or platform.

relations.mechanism: Fatal or repeated hardware errors can reset, remove, or disable the matching device instance.
when: Hardware source identity and PnP device identity refer to the same component.
symptoms: Device disappears, resets, or reports a problem code.
counter: The hardware record maps elsewhere and the device remains healthy.
limits: Identity mapping must use real topology or identifiers, not labels alone.

relations.mechanism: Severe performance reduction under thermal limiting can stretch synchronous work and make an application appear unresponsive.
when: Limiting overlaps the hang and application work is CPU or GPU bound.
symptoms: Performance collapse without process termination.
counter: No limiting occurs or the application is blocked on an unrelated wait.
limits: Thread and hardware telemetry are needed for strong attribution.

relations.mechanism: Storage controller or bus failures can produce hardware errors alongside disk and file-system symptoms.
when: WHEA topology maps to the storage controller or attached device.
symptoms: I/O errors, resets, or storage disappearance.
counter: The hardware record maps to an unrelated component.
limits: Disk health metadata and WHEA cover different failure layers.

relations.mechanism: Errors in a GPU or its PCIe path can make CUDA initialization or execution fail.
when: The WHEA or device event maps to the CUDA-visible GPU and time aligns.
symptoms: Device lost, initialization error, or workload termination.
counter: The GPU path is healthy and the failure is explained by software compatibility or memory pressure.
limits: CUDA error messages alone do not prove physical hardware failure.

relations.mechanism: Explicit Defender health events can report stopped protection, stale intelligence, or engine and service failures.
when: The current product event reports an unhealthy state.
symptoms: Protection unavailable or update failure.
counter: A current healthy report and running required services weaken the failure hypothesis.
limits: A healthy event is point-in-time and does not prove complete threat protection.

relations.mechanism: Multiple management authorities or effective policy can place Defender in an unexpected disabled or passive configuration.
when: Effective policy and Defender state conflict with intended management.
symptoms: Real-time protection disabled or settings revert.
counter: One authoritative policy produces the intended effective state.
limits: Policy inventory can require organization-specific management context.

relations.mechanism: Controlled Folder Access or another security control can intentionally block a process from modifying a protected location.
when: A Defender event identifies the exact process and protected target.
symptoms: Write denied despite normal file-system health.
counter: No relevant block event exists and ordinary ACL evaluation denies the operation.
limits: The reference does not authorize exclusions or weakening protection.

relations.mechanism: Quarantine or execution prevention can remove or block a component required by an application.
when: The security event names the exact binary or dependency used by the application.
symptoms: Startup failure or missing component.
counter: The required component is present and no matching security action occurred.
limits: Security detections must not be overridden by the investigator.

relations.mechanism: Connectivity failure to security-intelligence endpoints can prevent Defender intelligence updates.
when: Update errors identify connectivity and the effective proxy path is failing.
symptoms: Security intelligence age increases or update event fails.
counter: Defender endpoints are reachable and intelligence updates succeed.
limits: Engine and platform failures can prevent updates despite healthy networking.

relations.mechanism: Antimalware scanning can consume CPU during active scans or intensive file activity.
when: Defender process activity and scan events account for measured CPU load.
symptoms: Temporary CPU pressure and application slowdown.
counter: Defender processes are idle while another process accounts for load.
limits: Do not infer a security defect from expected bounded scan activity.

relations.mechanism: Pending servicing actions may need restart completion before another update can proceed normally.
when: Servicing explicitly records restart required before the failing attempt.
symptoms: Update remains pending or installation cannot finalize.
counter: No pending actions exist and the system restarted after the prior update.
limits: Pending restart state can coexist with an unrelated update error.

relations.mechanism: Corruption or inconsistency in the component store can prevent package staging or servicing transactions.
when: CBS or DISM health evidence identifies component-store corruption.
symptoms: Servicing failure across one or more packages.
counter: Component-store health checks complete cleanly and failure is package-specific.
limits: A servicing error code must be interpreted with current CBS context.

relations.mechanism: An update built for another product, build, architecture, or prerequisite level is not applicable to the current system.
when: Package applicability metadata conflicts with the observed OS inventory.
symptoms: Not applicable or prerequisite failure.
counter: Edition, build, architecture, and prerequisites match the package.
limits: Exact package applicability can change with supersedence and servicing metadata.

relations.mechanism: Loss of DNS, route, proxy, firewall, or TLS connectivity can prevent update scan and download phases.
when: Servicing reports a transport error and network failure occurs first.
symptoms: Scan or download fails before installation.
counter: Payload is already local or endpoint transport succeeds.
limits: Network evidence does not explain failures during installation or commit.

relations.mechanism: A failed or incomplete driver update can leave active and intended driver versions different.
when: The failed package targets the exact device driver and version inventory confirms mismatch.
symptoms: Old driver remains active or device requires restart.
counter: The active driver matches the successfully installed intended package.
limits: Not every driver version difference is harmful.

relations.mechanism: Failure to apply platform or intelligence updates can leave a security component outdated or unable to report current health.
when: The failed package is a required security platform or intelligence update.
symptoms: Stale security component version or health warning.
counter: The security component and intelligence are current despite the unrelated update failure.
limits: Update age alone is not evidence of compromise.

relations.mechanism: Windows loader search can fail when a required DLL is absent from the applicable safe search locations.
when: Loader evidence identifies the exact missing dependency.
symptoms: Application fails before main initialization.
counter: The exact dependency resolves and loads from the expected location.
limits: The investigator does not search arbitrary filesystem paths.

relations.mechanism: A process cannot load a native module built for an incompatible processor architecture.
when: Process and dependency machine architectures are incompatible.
symptoms: Bad image format or immediate load failure.
counter: Process and every required native dependency use compatible architectures.
limits: Architecture inventory must refer to the actual loaded binary, not a product label.

relations.mechanism: An application can require a runtime ABI, entry point, or package version not provided by the installed environment.
when: The application requirement and installed runtime version are explicitly incompatible.
symptoms: Missing entry point, import error, or startup failure.
counter: A supported runtime version and required entry points are present.
limits: Version number difference alone is insufficient without a compatibility requirement.

relations.mechanism: The loader may terminate application startup when a required library cannot be resolved or initialized.
when: Failure occurs in the load phase before application logic.
symptoms: Immediate exit or loader dialog.
counter: The application reaches normal initialization with all dependencies loaded.
limits: WER can name a module without proving search-order failure.

relations.mechanism: Application control or security policy can deny loading an otherwise present executable or module.
when: A policy enforcement event identifies the exact blocked binary.
symptoms: Startup or module-load failure.
counter: No relevant enforcement event exists and the binary is allowed.
limits: The investigator must not propose bypassing security policy.

relations.mechanism: CUDA applications depend on compatible user-mode runtime libraries in addition to the kernel driver.
when: The failing process cannot load the required CUDA runtime or dependent library.
symptoms: CUDA application fails before device execution.
counter: Required runtime libraries load and failure occurs later in device initialization.
limits: Toolkit installation is not required for every redistributable-based application.

relations.mechanism: A CUDA application requires a driver compatible with the toolkit/runtime features used by that application.
when: Observed driver and runtime versions fall outside NVIDIA's supported compatibility path.
symptoms: Initialization failure or call-requires-newer-driver error.
counter: Driver and runtime satisfy the documented compatibility requirements.
limits: Nominal version compatibility does not guarantee every feature or library combination.

relations.mechanism: A CUDA allocation fails when the workload requests more device memory than is available after existing allocations and runtime overhead.
when: Measured free VRAM is below the requested allocation at failure time.
symptoms: Out-of-memory error or model load failure.
counter: Sufficient contiguous usable device memory is available and allocation still fails for another reason.
limits: A point-in-time snapshot can miss transient allocations and allocator fragmentation.

relations.mechanism: Process environment or runtime selection can expose no usable CUDA device even when Windows detects a display adapter.
when: OS device inventory sees the GPU but the CUDA runtime reports no visible device.
symptoms: No device or CPU fallback.
counter: The target process enumerates the intended CUDA device.
limits: Visibility controls can be intentional and process-specific.

relations.mechanism: An active NVIDIA driver older than the minimum required by the CUDA runtime can invalidate the supported compatibility path.
when: Exact active driver and runtime versions violate the published matrix.
symptoms: Initialization or feature availability error.
counter: The active driver meets the required version and feature path.
limits: Do not infer incompatibility from marketing CUDA labels alone; record exact versions.

relations.mechanism: Memory pressure can force eviction, fallback, retry, or serialized execution that appears as an application stall before an explicit error.
when: GPU memory saturation overlaps the stall and the workload uses that GPU.
symptoms: Long model load or inference pause.
counter: GPU memory has adequate headroom and the workload is blocked elsewhere.
limits: VRAM utilization alone cannot distinguish useful allocation from pathological pressure.

relations.mechanism: A GPU reset, removal, or PCIe fault can make a previously visible CUDA device unavailable to a process.
when: Matching GPU device or WHEA errors precede the visibility change.
symptoms: Device lost or no device after reset.
counter: The GPU remains healthy and visible to the same runtime context.
limits: Process-specific visibility configuration can mimic hardware disappearance.

relations.mechanism: A configured in-game or driver maximum frame rate can hold game-produced frames near that ceiling even when GPU capacity is available.
when: An independently measured game frame rate plateaus near an exact configured cap under otherwise comparable load.
symptoms: Stable low FPS despite available graphics headroom.
counter: Frame rate remains far below the configured cap while the game is actively rendering.
limits: Current registered probes do not collect in-game or driver frame-cap settings or independent game frame times; low GPU utilization alone does not prove a cap.
applies: windows gaming with configurable frame limiter

relations.mechanism: A display updating at a lower active refresh rate can make game motion look less smooth even if the game produces frames faster than the display can show.
when: The complaint is about displayed motion and measured game-produced FPS exceeds active display refresh.
symptoms: Poor perceived smoothness despite adequate rendered FPS.
counter: A reliable game counter measures 12 FPS while the display runs at 60 Hz or higher; display refresh alone does not explain that render-rate collapse.
limits: The display.mode probe reports only the calling desktop's current mode, not the game's display, dynamic refresh changes, or game frame times; this is not a cause of genuinely low measured render FPS.

relations.mechanism: On a multi-adapter system, a game rendering on an unintended lower-performance GPU may deliver fewer frames than when it renders on the intended adapter.
when: The same game process is mapped to an unintended GPU engine while the higher-performance adapter is available, and a comparable run shows a material frame-time difference.
symptoms: Low FPS with the intended GPU comparatively idle.
counter: Per-process GPU-engine evidence shows the game actually renders on the intended adapter.
limits: Current registered probes inventory adapters and NVIDIA aggregate telemetry but do not identify the game's render engine; Windows app GPU preference can override NVIDIA Control Panel preference.
applies: windows client with multiple graphics adapters

relations.mechanism: A driver regression, unsupported graphics feature, or failed installation can reduce game performance, but a version number by itself is not a diagnosis.
when: A repeatable performance regression begins with a driver change or device problem and matched game workload measurements exclude stronger alternatives.
symptoms: Lower FPS or new stutter after a graphics-stack change.
counter: The same driver and game workload previously produced normal frame times, or the slowdown predates the driver change.
limits: Current probes do not benchmark the game, identify feature-specific driver regressions, or establish a driver fault from update age alone.

relations.mechanism: NVIDIA reports software power capping as a clock-event reason when a GPU reduces requested graphics clocks to remain within its power envelope.
when: Power-cap reason and reduced graphics clocks recur during the affected game workload, with power draw interpreted against the reported limit.
symptoms: GPU clocks remain constrained during demand.
counter: Power-cap reason is inactive throughout comparable GPU-bound slow frames.
limits: NVIDIA telemetry fields and clock-event reasons may be unsupported, and a configured power envelope can be normal rather than faulty.
applies: windows client with supported nvidia telemetry

relations.mechanism: NVIDIA thermal slowdown mechanisms reduce graphics clocks when GPU thermal control is active.
when: Thermal clock-event reason, temperature, and lower graphics clocks coincide with the affected workload over repeated samples.
symptoms: Falling graphics clocks during sustained game load.
counter: Thermal slowdown remains inactive while clocks and game frame times are degraded.
limits: Temperature alone is not proof of throttling; three short aggregate samples can miss brief episodes and do not measure game frame times.
applies: windows client with supported nvidia telemetry

relations.mechanism: When a game is limited by its render GPU, sustained reduction in available graphics clocks can lengthen frame rendering time.
when: The game is shown to be GPU-bound and its low frame rate overlaps an active clock-limiting reason on the same adapter.
symptoms: Lower game FPS during the clock-limited interval.
counter: The game is CPU-bound, frame-capped, or uses another adapter while the sampled GPU clocks are low.
limits: Idle GPUs lower clocks normally; current telemetry does not prove the game's GPU-bound status or measure its frames.
applies: windows gaming with supported gpu telemetry

relations.mechanism: Competing CPU work can delay simulation, draw-call preparation, or frame submission while a capable GPU waits for new work.
when: Per-process CPU pressure overlaps low game frame rate, and the game's render GPU is not the saturated stage.
symptoms: Low FPS with high competing CPU activity and relatively low GPU load.
counter: CPU activity is low throughout the bad interval and frame time is dominated by GPU execution.
limits: Overall CPU percentage can hide a busy game thread; current samples do not attribute per-frame CPU/GPU time.

relations.mechanism: A second GPU workload can compete with game rendering for scheduled GPU engines or graphics memory on the same adapter.
when: Per-process GPU-engine activity identifies competing work on the game's adapter during slow game frames.
symptoms: Intermittent FPS loss while another GPU workload runs.
counter: The game is the only significant user of the relevant GPU engine during the bad interval.
limits: Current NVIDIA aggregate telemetry and process inventory do not attribute engine use to the competing process; temporal overlap alone is not causation.

relations.mechanism: A game's graphics allocations can compete for dedicated GPU memory and may incur costly transfers or fallback when the working set exceeds available residency.
when: Dedicated-memory pressure and game frame-time spikes coincide, with the game identified as a material allocator on the same GPU.
symptoms: Stutter or low FPS when memory-intensive scenes or other GPU workloads appear.
counter: Dedicated memory has ample headroom during the same slow scenes and no relevant allocation churn occurs.
limits: Total VRAM used is not per-game usage or proof of eviction; current probes do not measure graphics residency or frame-time spikes.
applies: windows gaming with dedicated or shared gpu memory

relations.mechanism: When a game produces few frames per second, the display cannot show new game frames more often than they are produced, regardless of the display's maximum refresh setting.
when: Independent frame-time measurements confirm slow game-produced frames during the user's complaint.
symptoms: Visible stutter or sluggish game motion.
counter: Game-produced frame times are normal while only presentation or display refresh appears slow.
limits: Current registered probes do not directly capture per-game frame times or presentation pacing.
